summary: Oxazepam is a short-to-intermediate-acting benzodiazepine used for anxiety disorders, short-term relief of anxiety symptoms, and anxiety/agitation in alcohol withdrawal. Because it is conjugated directly (no oxidative metabolism) to inactive metabolites, it is often favoured in the elderly and in liver disease. It carries a boxed warning regarding concomitant opioid use, abuse/misuse/addiction, and dependence/withdrawal. It is a Schedule IV controlled substance and is habit forming.

Anxiety, tension, agitation and irritability in older patients

moa: Oxazepam enhances the inhibitory action of gamma-aminobutyric acid (GABA) at the GABA-A receptor by binding the benzodiazepine site, increasing the frequency of chloride channel opening. This hyperpolarises neurons and produces anxiolytic, sedative, muscle-relaxant, and anticonvulsant effects. It is metabolised by direct glucuronidation to inactive products.

preg: Avoid in pregnancy. Benzodiazepine use, especially in late pregnancy, risks neonatal sedation, hypotonia (floppy infant syndrome), feeding difficulties, and withdrawal. Use only if clearly essential with specialist input.
lact: Avoid during breastfeeding; oxazepam is excreted in breast milk and may cause sedation, poor feeding, and weight loss in the infant.
renal: Generally tolerated in renal impairment because its metabolites are inactive, but use with caution and monitor for excess sedation.
hepatic: Often a preferred benzodiazepine in hepatic impairment because it is conjugated directly without oxidative (CYP) metabolism, reducing accumulation; nevertheless use cautiously and at lower doses in significant liver disease.

interactions.diagnostics: Detectable as benzodiazepine on urine drug screens

pearls: Schedule IV controlled substance - HABIT FORMING; boxed warning for opioid co-use, abuse/addiction, and dependence/withdrawal
Metabolised by direct glucuronidation (no oxidative metabolism), making it a preferred benzodiazepine in liver disease and the elderly
Slower onset than diazepam/alprazolam - less euphoric 'rush', lower abuse appeal but still controlled

missed: Take the missed dose as soon as you remember unless it is almost time for the next dose, in which case skip it - do not double up. If you miss several doses, do not restart at a higher dose; contact your prescriber and never stop abruptly.
overdose: Overdose causes drowsiness, confusion, slurred speech, ataxia, and in severe cases (especially with alcohol or opioids) respiratory depression, hypotension and coma. Management is supportive with airway/ventilatory support; the benzodiazepine antagonist flumazenil may be used cautiously but can precipitate seizures in dependent patients or mixed overdoses.
